body: I think [permissions policy](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Permissions_Policy) is probably a better fit, as it doesn't require opting into the whole sandboxing infrastructure. What do you think?

The goal would be for this to be allowed by default to ensure accessibility coverage, and then authors can disallow it as they see fit. Is that possible with permissions policy? I was under the impression that it was the opposite (disallowed by default, and authors allow as they see fit).
Yes, if you set a default allowlist of `*`, then authors can override that with `<iframe allow="aria-notify 'none'">` or `Permissions-Policy: aria-notify=(self)`.
Ah I see, if we are able to make it allowed by default using `*`, then that approach sounds reasonable to me
Isn't Document Policy better here (since ARIA Notify doesn't need a permission I assume)?

@zcorpan The idea would be that `ariaNotify()` is allowed by default to embedded iframes, but gives authors a way to prevent this as they see fit. What are the pros and cons of using Document Policy vs a permission policy for this?

The differences between the two are explained [here](https://wicg.github.io/document-policy/#relation-to-permissions-policy). I think permissions policy is a reasonable fit. (Despite the name, it's unrelated to browser permissions; that naming compromise was because someone didn't like the original name "feature policy".)

But, the proposers should check that the fit is correct, e.g. behaviors such as

>  Permissions Policy features are boolean-valued (either enabled or disabled), can never be re-enabled in a child frame if disabled in its parent, and generally follow the model of "available in top-level browsing contexts and their same-origin children; must be delegated to cross-origin frames."

(Although as discussed above, this last part is over-general. If you set your default allowlist to `*` instead of `self`, a different behavior obtains.)

Thanks @domenic for this link, that helps provide clarity on when to use which.

Based on this distinction, I agree that Permission Policy seems like the better fit in this case, and confirm that the below matches the desired intention:

> Permissions Policy features are boolean-valued (either enabled or disabled), can never be re-enabled in a child frame if disabled in its parent, and generally follow the model of "available in top-level browsing contexts and their same-origin children; must be delegated to cross-origin frames."

Thanks @zcorpan and @domenic for the suggestions. I'm wondering if this may be something we could get an async resolution on?

I think the only browser we haven't heard from is Safari. @annevk any thoughts on the above proposal (with the adjustment to use permission policy per https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11004#issuecomment-2641306814)?

Also happy to add this to the agenda if preferred.

> "it's unrelated to browser permissions"

That's not true? The Permissions API is used for used for everything in Permissions Policy as well. Or are you only talking about permissions that are exposed to end users, which is a decision that browsers make on their own as it's UX-related?

By "browser permissions" I indeed meant permissions exposed to end users.

https://w3c.github.io/permissions/#relationship-to-permissions-policy explains the relationship between permissions policy and the permissions API (both of which are unrelated to browser permissions).

(I'm not sure I'd state it quite as strongly as "unrelated", but there's definitely certain permissions you'd probably not expose directly.)

I don't really like using Permissions Policy for things that are enabled by default in cross-origin documents as that can then be used to unexpectedly alter the control flow in such documents. Document Policy is usually a better fit for such cases as the embedded document will have to agree to the restrictions (or result in not loading).

> I don't really like using Permissions Policy for things that are enabled by default in cross-origin documents as that can then be used to unexpectedly alter the control flow in such documents. Document Policy is usually a better fit for such cases as the embedded document will have to agree to the restrictions (or result in not loading).

First, probably the most important point: in this particular case, I don't think it has to alter control flow. IIUC, there is no signal back to the page as to whether the `ariaNotify()` call "worked". The proposal is very clear that there is no readback of that.

So, if we spec that when `ariaNotify()` is disallowed by permissions policy, the API simply does nothing (instead of throwing an exception), then I think your concern is mitigated.

---

The rest of this post is about the general permissions policy vs. document policy question, and is perhaps off-topic given the above. But let me include it anyway in case it's useful for future discussions.

I am sympathetic to this concern. However, in practice I don't feel things have turned out quite as you've hoped. Nobody has implemented the parts of document policy that allow for negotiation between subframes and parent frames (i.e., `Require-Document-Policy`/`Sec-Required-Document-Policy`/`<iframe policy="">`). Largely because, no feature author is interested in creating a feature which causes ~all subframes on the web to stop working, until server operators upgrade them to respond to this protocol.

I'm skeptical that the ARIA folks want to be the first such feature. It would mean:

- Getting those parts of the Document Policy spec implemented in browsers.
- Making website authors who want to restrict aria-notify on subframes responsible for evangelizing to all their subframes that they need to implement this new header-based protocol for restricting themselves.

If we restrict ourselves to only available technologies, I think we have the following choices:

- `<iframe sandbox>`. This has mostly negatives:
  - It is, by design, a mechanism for the parent to alter control flow in cross-origin subframes, so your original concern is not addressed.
  - It means the syntax for page authors to disable only aria notify is `<iframe sandbox="allow-downloads allow-forms allow-modals allow-orientation-lock allow-pointer-lock allow-popups allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox allow-presentation allow-same-origin allow-scripts allow-storage-access-by-user-activation allow-top-navigation allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation allow-top-navigation-to-custom-protocols">`, which is a bit unwieldy.
  - It means page authors can only restrict aria notify on subframes if they are OK also restricting all future features we might add to sandbox.
  - It means that all existing `<iframe sandbox>` deployments automatically cannot use aria notify, which might not be intended.
- Permissions policy with a default allowlist of `'self'`:
  - Does not allow subframes by default, which is maybe over-restrictive
- Permissions policy with a default allowlist of `*`:
  - Allows parents to alter control flow in cross-origin subframes (in cases where we decide the result is an exception)

Note that document policy is not on the list, as no implemented version of document policy lets parents control their child frame's behavior.

Thanks @domenic for the detailed explanation. Based on this, we will plan to move forward with prototyping and putting a draft spec update together for the permission policy solution.

@annevk and @zcorpan please let us know, though, if you have any outstanding objections to this approach.

If there is indeed no influence possible over control flow I think my concern is mitigated. Though I'm still not a big fan of permissions that are auto-granted to cross-origin documents. (Perhaps that is an option we should seek to eliminate from Permissions Policy.)

Colleagues working on accessibility have concerns with the overall proposal I believe, but will raise those in the relevant forum.

> Though I'm still not a big fan of permissions that are auto-granted to cross-origin documents. (Perhaps that is an option we should seek to eliminate from Permissions Policy.)

I am curious why this is problematic? Permissions in the general sense of the word can be either granted or denied. What reasoning do you see for removing the ability for permissions that are allowed by default? It seems reasonable to me for permissions to have the ability to be opt-out or opt-in.

As permissions gate something powerful, it should be up to the document that carries the authority from the end user's perspective (through the address bar), whether such permissions can be requested by documents that do not carry such authority, so that blame flows in the appropriate manner.

I agree that we need to be careful about the direction in which permissions are allowed/granted, however, I still am unclear on why it is problematic to allow a permission by default if it makes sense for that scenario.

In the case of `ariaNotify()`, for example, we want this to be allowed by default to ensure that content is accessible by default, unless content is deemed to be causing more harm than good with their use of the feature. Are you suggesting that it would make more sense for this permission to not be allowed by default, or that there is some reason that permission policies in general shouldn't allow this pattern?

It seems extremely unlikely that a top-level document will take adequate care to revoke this permission from malicious ads (that it might not even know are being displayed), but it seems quite likely it will grant this permission to cooperating embeds.

My concern is that if we don't make this allowed by default, there will certainly be cases where embedders will forget to enable this (probably more often than not), resulting in a poorer experience for AT users without them knowing they are missing out on information. There are lots of embedding scenarios outside of ads, for example, where I would assume usage of `ariaNotify` will be higher.

In the converse scenario (allowing by default), if there is abuse, noise or malicious content being announced w/ `ariaNotify`, AT users would be able to flag it to the site owner to aid them in opting out of this behavior.

I would tend to optimize for making content accessible by default and allowing for this to be turned off in (hopefully) edge case "bad" scenarios.

Could we rather fix the API somehow so that it can't cause the bad scenarios in cross-origin iframes?
It feels rather unlikely that sites would remember to disable the feature when needed (and many sites aren't too good at fixing issues in them even if users report them).

> Could we rather fix the API somehow so that it can't cause the bad scenarios in cross-origin iframes?

We have some ideas for continuing to provide authors with opportunities to reduce noise, but these mechanisms would require both authors to opt into these functionalities, and requires ATs to do something with the new functionality. I'd suggest taking a look at the explainer for future considerations we're working on in this area: https://github.com/MicrosoftEdge/MSEdgeExplainers/blob/main/Accessibility/AriaNotify/explainer.md#future-considerations.

There is also an open issue to explore this further: https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues/2499.

In general, we think this API should actually result in lest noise/bad behaviors as compared to live regions (which is what authors are using today as a workaround to accomplish custom notification handling for AT users). The reason being that with `ariaNotify`, authors will need to be fairly explicit to introduce bad behaviors, whereas with live regions, it is more ambiguous to authors when they are using it incorrectly, leading to noisier user experiences without their knowledge.

Either way, if authors intend to do something "bad" they can already do so with live regions, with or without the `ariaNotify` API, but we're hoping to give authors more mechanisms to do this right with this new API, hence, also having a way for authors to opt out for embedded content, as needed.

If you have any particular ideas on improving this within the API itself, please let us know or feel free to post in https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues/2499 or file a new issue within the [ARIA github page](https://github.com/w3c/aria/issues).
